utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Joanna Korner, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence. Our client is not present. He will come after the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do have a matter to raise before the first witness today is called. Although Mr. Olmsted is -- is going to be calling the witness, Your Honours, it really raises a matter of principle, which is why I'm here dealing with. Your Honours will have seen that the next witness was in the motion called to deal with some two adjudicated facts that were denied or -- or in some way altered. I hope Your Honours had a chance to look at the proofing note that was sent round last week, because Your Honours will see that it is proposed that he give evidence on, in fact, a total of seven adjudicated facts. Your Honours, the fact is that's the evidence he can give. And it's our submission that although originally we put him down only for the three, he should be allowed to give evidence about all of them, for this reason: Your Honours, effectively, if we call witnesses who can speak to other adjudicated facts which were the subject of, as I say, either rejection or alteration by the Trial Chamber, then they should be allowed to do so. Clearly it's in Your Honours' interest to have the best evidence available when you come to render your decision in this case. And, of course, the adjudicated facts which come from the trial or appeal judgements are a distillation, quite often, of large numbers of witnesses having given that evidence and/or documents. In addition, Your Honour, the adjudicated facts, until a slight change in the Defence position, which has been coming about very recently, have not been agreed. In other words, they're the subject of either putting the Prosecution to strict proof or direct challenge that the events contained in the adjudicated facts ever happened. And so, therefore, it's important that the Prosecution is able to prove those matters to the best of its ability. Your Honour, we submit the only, as it were, flaw would be the question of notice, and we say it's not a flaw because we have given 65 ter summaries for each of these witnesses which show the matters that they can speak about. And, in addition, they'll be shown in the proofing note, which in this case I believe was delivered Thursday -- yes, Thursday of last week. So, Your Honours, in all the circumstances, we say that the witness, particularly this witness -- because some of the adjudicated facts relate to the context of how he comes to deal with the actual facts for which he was originally notified, and Your Honours have said we can lead evidence as to context. So in all circumstances, Your Honour, we say, and we're raising it now because it's going to happen with some other witnesses as well, so that we can have a ruling from Your Honours whether we may be allowed to do this. So, Your Honour, that's the submission we make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do object to this, and I will give our reasons right now. The 16th of June motion -- the Prosecutor's motion says, paragraph 4: "The denied adjudicated fact in essence provides the summaries of the facts on which the proposed witness will provide evidence." So if that is a position -- that was the position of the Office of the Prosecutor, at that point they should have stated all the adjudicated facts that they intend to prove through that witness. So if they failed to do that, there is really nothing we can do about it. They are supposed to know their case, and they are supposed to know what their witnesses are going to testify -- or are able to give evidence about. The Trial Chamber decision of 14th July says, paragraph 20: "The Trial Chamber reiterates that the testimony of each selected proposed witness will be admissible solely for the limited purpose of seeking to establish the substance of the specified denied adjudicated fact." Your Honours, if what Ms. Korner just said, it's important that the Prosecution is able to prove those matters to the best of its ability - it's page 2; 24, 25, lines. Now, as I said, if this is important for the Office of the Prosecutor, they should have, at the point on the 16th of June, they should have proposed all these witnesses and specified the exact adjudicated facts that they -- these witnesses are going to give the evidence about. In this -- doing it at this point is highly prejudicial for the Defence, and the Defence had no notice about it, whether the -- if the Office of the Prosecutor is going to raise additional adjudicated facts with -- with these witnesses. This creates a problem for us, you see, Your Honours, because some of the witnesses which came earlier we could have challenged the adjudicated facts, have we been on notice that the -- that the -- that the Office of the Prosecutor is willing to bring the -- the evidence to that effect. Therefore -- therefore, we take the -- the objection very seriously, and we -- and we very serious object to this line of -- of conducting the case by the Office of the Prosecutor. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, very shortly, adopting the position of Stanisic Defence, I would like to outline the practice imposed by the OTP in this case with amendments of 65 ter list, amendments of the -- in terms of evidence, in terms of documents, in terms of witnesses, and now we have another attempt to sort of say on the backdoor introduce certain elements of the theory of their case. Obviously so big confusion in presenting of OTP case is actually on place, and the mere fact that they filed more than 50 motions in terms of the amendment of the initial 65 ter list practical every -- every week, the average is number -- every week, one motion, plus this approach with adjudicated facts issue which is absolutely in contravention of the rulings and the orders of this Trial Chamber. Shortly, if this kind of request will be granted, that would be a serious violation of the -- of the principles of the fairness of the trial and the interests of the accused. That's the point. We have to -- to know, and we're asking -- kindly ask from this Trial Chamber to -- to tell the OTP to stop. We have to know where is the line, where is the moment to stop in this kind of practice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, for the record, this witness was called only for -- for a -- one adjudicated fact, which is 470. And I don't see really to -- the reason for expansion in terms of the -- the issue of -- of judicial economy, in terms of issue of the trial expedition in terms of costs, in terms of the issue of repetitiveness, because we -- we see that many of these witnesses will -- will tell the same story, so I think all these facts should be -- should be -- have in mind before reaching the decision. Thank you so much for your attention, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you indicate the seven new facts that you are raising.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours haven't got the proofing not with you? Your Honour, the facts that this witness will be called for are 263, 470, 471, 860, 861, 875, 1082. As I say, part of it is the -- is the actual context as well of how this witness -- would Your Honours give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- this witness is going to deal with the killings outside of Manjaca, but he comes from Omarska. And these -- some of these adjudicated facts deal with Omarska. Now, Your Honours, can I just answer two matters raised by Mr. Zecevic, which is this: First of all, notice. As I say, we argue there is notice, originally in the 65 ter but in the proofing note which was handed out on Thursday. And, Your Honour, these are crime-based witnesses, all of them, and we would submit that that's -- you know, 48 -- sorry, 48 -- 72 hours' worth is sufficient notice. Second matter, I don't quite understand what Mr. Zecevic means by "some of the witnesses which came earlier we could have challenged the adjudicated facts, have we been on notice that the Office of the Prosecutor is willing to bring evidence" about them. Well, Your Honours they have -- those adjudicated facts that they have taken issue with, they have been challenging. And we've always made it clear that where an adjudicated fact was challenged we would be calling the evidence which related to that adjudicated fact. So I don't quite follow what Mr. Zecevic means by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you like me to explain, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor proposed some adjudicated facts. The Trial Chamber decided on the adjudicated facts. After the decision on adjudicated facts, the witness -- the Office of the Prosecutor asked by their motion to add additional witnesses to deal with some of the adjudicated facts that have been -- that have not been accepted by the Trial Chamber or accepted in full. Now, out of, let's say, hundred of the adjudicated facts which originally were proposed, the Office of the Prosecutor calls witnesses for 20 or 50 adjudicated facts. So other 50, they're not calling any evidence. Therefore, why should we challenge these facts if they are not going to be part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think there's a slight misunderstanding there, Your Honours. These are all -- these are not adjudicated facts which have been accepted, these adjudicated facts are ones which have been, as I say, either denied or in some way tinkered with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But that is precisely the point which I'm trying to explain to Your Honours. Had we been on notice that the Prosecutor is willing to bring evidence about these adjudicated facts, then we would have raised that with some of the witnesses which passed in the meantime between the 16th of June and today [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, there's still a - sorry - there's still misunderstanding. All of these facts are in our annex but covered by other witnesses. Sorry, they're not adjudicated facts; they're all ones from the annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank counsel for their submissions. It seems to us that there is eminent logic in the application that is made by the Office of the Prosecution; and had the application, as articulated today, been the subject of the earlier motion dealing with these witnesses, that it would have been difficult to not accede to that application. However, the Chamber, having ruled on how the witnesses who are being called in respect of the denied adjudicated facts, how their evidence should be limited and circumscribed, we find ourselves in total agreement with the first part of Mr. Zecevic's reply. And, therefore, our Ruling is that, to confirm our earlier decision, that the witnesses who are being called in respect of the adjudicated facts, that the evidence would be limited to the specified adjudicated facts and so much of the context as is necessary to make sense of it. And the -- that allowance of context is not an invitation to lead the witness far afield beyond the limitations of the specified adjudicated facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, one other matter. I'm reminded that the next witness, we filed a motion to dealing with the protective measures of all the new witnesses some time ago, ST-017 has protective measures, which were granted in two earlier cases, and I'm assuming that Your Honours will therefore be carrying on the protective measures for him, which are pseudonym and closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. That -- that motion is in the process of being refined, but the principle, of course, is that such protective measures as have been afford previously would continue to apply.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, while we're on the subject of still outstanding motions, Your Honour, we still haven't had rulings on a number of - I think it's about three - witnesses that we've applied to call to deal with matters. And, obviously, we are actually getting near the end of the case, and I don't know the order of priority in Your Honours dealing with motions, but obviously the application to call witnesses are clearly quite important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We thank you for the reminder, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, while we are waiting for the witness to be escorted to the court, I kindly ask our friends, I think it's in the interest of both sides also and Trial Chamber, that before the examination of particular witness just for the record we have a reference of which fact, adjudicated fact, we are having this particular witness. If it's not a big problem, I mean. And then we could easily follow, at a later stage, what is relevant, what -- if -- if it's not big complication. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought we had that, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean before -- after the solemn declaration then, I mean -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I -- I now -- yes, I now see what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- and then we could later on follow the issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That would be convenient. I now follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- to add to what I would have said before, the -- if the Prosecution is minded to adopt such a procedure - and I don't know that we would require them to do so - of course, it would have to occur before the witness is escorted to the stand, for obvious reasons. Yes, please have the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. I trust that can you hear me in a language that you understand. The solemn declaration that you have just made imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony to this Tribunal. And should you fail to do so, the Tribunal is empowered to impose penalties for perjury under the statutes which created the Tribunal. Would you begin by telling us your name, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Muharem Murselovic. I live in Prijedor where I was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your date of birth and what is your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 24th of November, 1947, in Prijedor. I'm a Bosniak by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an economist in the catering business. That's my profession. And that's what I did until the war. After the war, I was in politics. I held an office in local politics, and for the past -- for the last three years I've --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: For the last three years I have been an MP in the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified before this Tribunal in the Stakic case and in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. In which case I need only remind you of our procedure and that is that the side calling begins by questioning and then the side opposite has the right to cross-examine. And the side calling you then has a right to ask questions in re-direct. And the Chamber may, at any point, intervene to ask questions by way of clarification. I'm sorry, could counsel for each of the accused indicate what their estimate of the time is that they would need with this witness? We don't have it before us. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, most probably, the Stanisic Defence will not have any questions for this witness unless there should be an issue in his statement. In that case, we will require perhaps up to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic. Sorry. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will cross-examine this witness Your Honour. To be on the safe side, maximum 40, 45 minutes for this witness. Even less if this issue of context will be narrow. But context, with our friends from the OTP is very relative issue. So if we shall speak about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- 470, that's okay. But if something will arise, then I reserve my application for more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just very quickly, that is a matter, actually, that I had intended to raise. We've actually not been given any cross-examination estimates, and we need -- our planning is dependant on what cross-examination is going to be. I wonder if Your Honours would care to order that we now get cross-examination estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is an issue you may recall, Ms. Korner, that we have been considering and turning over in our minds for some time. And I confess it has been put somewhat on the back burner because we have discovered that it is not a -- it is not as easily done as first appears. But it's something that we haven't forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, how long -- we do have some estimates before us, but we take it that was in anticipation of the success of the motion which had been earlier made. What is your revised estimate of time that you would spend in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Considerably less. I think we'll probably be going around an hour, maybe a little bit more, depending on how much this witness -- how long his answers are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Witness, I had interrupted the preliminary questions that the Bench puts to you to get an estimate of the time that it would -- is expected your testimony would take. And you would have heard what has passed between the Bench and counsel and therefore I needn't repeat it. The only thing that I would add is that the sitting times of the Court are from when we have a morning session we rise for the day at 1.45 but the -- each session is of no more than 90 minutes because the tapes have to be changed in order to -- for the record-keeping of the Tribunal. And the advantage of such breaks is that allows for the convenience of the Bench, counsel, witnesses, and everyone else. But notwithstanding those fixed periods when we would break in which the day's sitting is divided, if for any time you feel discomfort and need to take a break, you alert us and we will, of course, accommodate you. And, Mr. Olmsted, you may begin your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Murselovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me first start by apologising for holding you here over the weekend. We know that you have a number of important matters to attend to back at home, so we're going to try to get you on a plane as soon as possible. Can you tell us, where did you reside before the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Until the war, I lived in Prijedor. I lived in the town. And the last address where I resided at was the main street of Prijedor, before it was called Marshal Tito Street, number 43, after the war. And when I came back in 1998, the name of the street is the King Peter I - the liberator - Street, number 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict, did you own any businesses in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until 1992. Actually, to be more precise, from 1978 until 1992 I was in private business. I had a restaurant which was called Mursel. I also had a snack bar. And in those conditions, it was quite a good business because this was still in time of socialism. One of the restaurants was in my name, the other one was in my wife's name. Later I formed a company, and this company employed up to 15 employees. I was fairly successful in this kind of work, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned a little bit while ago that you are currently involved in politics. Were you also involved in politics prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: At first multi-party elections in 1990, I was elected to the local parliament. I was elected a deputy, representing a party, which we called the Party of Private Initiative, which gathered private business owners, businessmen, and then as -- from 1990 to 1992, until the beginning of the conflict, I was a representative in the municipal body. Let me just mention, this is from the multi-party elections in 1990. Before 1990, I was never involved in politics. I was not a member of the League of Communists. So only after 1990 did I actively start taking part in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify a couple of matters, you mentioned you were a representative in the municipality body. Would that be the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Prijedor Municipal Assembly, the local body of the municipality of Prijedor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could tell us what ethnicities were represented by the party you belonged to, this Party of Private Initiative?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: All the businessmen were there in our party more or less. There were people of different ethnic groups in the party. I was a Muslim. Of course, there were other ethnic groups as members. The president of the party -- I don't really remember exactly who it was, but I think it was a man from Doboj. He was a Croat. It was a small party which brought together private artisans, businessmen, tradesmen, and it was of multi-ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you arrested on 30 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 23rd of May for the first time. The 23rd of May, 1992. I spent the night in prison, in the Prijedor Police Station, actually. There were six or seven other people there with me. I was arrested a week later for the second time. This was on the 30th of May, after which I was taken to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who arrested you on the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 30th of May around maybe 1.00, something like that. A neighbour knocked. His name was Ranko Vujasinovic. He was a young man of maybe 25 at the time. I don't think he was 30 years old yet. I knew his parents because his grandfather had the same name Rajko [as interpreted] Vujasinovic. I know that well. He knocked on the door, on the ground floor door. He asked me to come outside. I came out. I was alone in the apartment, in the house. And he asked me to bring weapons with me if I had any. I had a legal revolver with a licence. I handed that to him, and then he asked me -- it was actually quite insolent and arrogant. He was taking all the neighbours from the neighbouring houses to a hotel across the street. It was called Hotel Balkan. There were about 2- or 300 people there, men, women, children. All of these people were there, and we spent two or three hours in that hotel that afternoon. This is right across the street from my house on the square in Prijedor, in the very centre of town. It's an old hotel, a relatively old hotel, called Hotel Balkan. It was opened in 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned Ranko Vujasinovic. Do you know what organ he worked for?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: He was a reserve police officer, and he was wearing a police uniform, as a reserve policeman. He wasn't an active policeman; I knew that. His house is some 100 to 120 metres away from mine. So he was a reserve policeman; I know that for sure. There was another reserve police officer there, but I remember this one because he was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were taken to Omarska camp that day. Can you tell us who actually transported you to Omarska? Who was in charge of that transportation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that we were in quite an uncomfortable position in this hotel. We didn't know where we were there, what we were doing there, what reason. There were elderly women there, children also. At one point, the policemen checked our IDs, but we all knew each other more or less. But they said that Muslims should be separated and go to one side, and the Croats and the Serbs should go to the other side. Of course, I went and stood on the side where the Muslims were standing, and the Croats. And then from our group, they separated people who looked older. They were perhaps in their 70s or something like that. They told us that we should go outside. We went out in front of the hotel. There were buses there. I could see three or four buses. We boarded the buses. The bus that I boarded, there were quite a few people that I knew there. There was an Asif Kapetanovic there, Sefik Terzic; these were all people from the town, my neighbours practically. At the front entrance, there was a policeman who was standing there. He was already retired. I didn't know at the time whether he was retired already or not. He is a year or so younger than me, or perhaps the same age as me. I know that his name is Grahovac. I knew it then. Stevo Grahovac; I think that was his name. He was standing at the front door. He had a machine-gun, a weapon, in his hands. We entered the bus -- I entered the buses. And then three or four buses were filled, and then we set off from in front of the Hotel Balkan, and we went to the right, along the Mose Pijade Street. That's what it was called at the time. Now the name is Akademika Raskovica, Academician Raskovic Street. We went -- we passed the court-house, and then we stopped in front of the police station. The bus stopped in front of the police station. This was our Prijedor police station. It also stopped in front of the municipal building. We waited for a bit there. And an unpleasant incident, as far as I was concerned, occurred there. I asked this policeman, I asked him, Where are we being taken? Where are we going? Why are we being taken away? It was not clear to us, first of all, why we were taken from our homes; and then, secondly where they were being taken in these buses. I could see the people were surprised, they were upset. This Grahovac just was shrugging his shoulders as if he didn't know where we were going. Like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions with regard to this so we can get through this a little quicker. I just want to go back. You said that you were at the hotel and they separated people into two groups. And I want to clarify, for the record, was one group to consist of the Muslims and Croats, while the other group consisted of Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after -- you mentioned that you asked the police where they were taking you. Did the police ever tell you where they were taking you that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were just shrugging their shoulders. They said they didn't know where they were taking us. They were very insolent. This Vujasinovic was quite insolent, and he said something that was not nice to one of the neighbours and I think he kicked him. The situation was quite unpleasant. I mean, this person could have been his grandfather, not even his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, eventually, these buses that were on, they arrived at Omarska camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long were you detained --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. We didn't know where we were going. I had never been to this Omarska camp before. We were not even taking the Banja Luka-Prijedor road where you would usually go. We went by a different route through some neighbourhood. At one point while we were passing through town we were lying on the floor. We saw a few houses that were set on fire. But, basically, we got to this camp. We didn't know it was a camp. We came to this mine. There were some business or administration buildings around, some work-shops. We didn't know where we were, why we were there. But, in any case, this is where we arrived. Later we found out that this was Omarska, the Omarska mine. I didn't have the opportunity to see it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us how long you were at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the Omarska camp until August 6th, when we were -- our names were called out again. There was a check. And then on the 6th of August, again we boarded some buses, and now we were in a more difficult situation because we all had dysentery. We were all in a terrible, exhausted state. We had all lost at least 25 to 30 kilos. And then on the 6th of August - I think that was one of the most difficult days of my life - we didn't know we were going. We were boarded on the buses at 10.00 in the morning, and we were travelling by placing our head forward. We were lying on the floor. And it was unbearably hot and the heat was turned on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. We are going to get to that incident in a little bit. I just want to lay a little more context so we understand that event clearly. During your time at Omarska, were you able to determine who was the commander at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, point number one: We have this adjudicated facts related to this question. I -- it slipped to my -- but it's not in dispute. We have it. You already ruled that it's adjudicated facts. Point number 2: If my learned friend Mr. Olmsted will go with these kinds of questioning relating to context, he will cover practically all facts which was previously denied and limited not to do that. What we have here, we have Mr. Murselovic, he was a victim, he suffered a lot, he has his story to tell, but specifically related to the incident out - I will not mention the name, the place - out of Omarska camp. So I think -- I didn't react before, but all these questions and answers are really -- are going nowhere in terms of the judicial economy and the efficiency of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to lay some foundation. Obviously the incident which occurred on the 6th of August, 1992, the 6th and 7th of August, 1992, we have to lay the foundation that he knew who were -- was involved in it, who was there that morning, who from the leadership at the camp was there. So I'm just laying foundation as to whether he knows who was at the camp, who was in charge, and what was happening that morning. And, of course, his time, for over two and a half months, would give him some insight as to who these particular individuals are. I'm not trying to expand into other adjudicated facts; I'm really just laying the context so we can understand his evidence with regard to the particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we trust that we aren't going to have to laboriously go through this each time one of the witnesses to testify to adjudicated facts is called. To repeat what we have said on more occasions than I would try to count, obviously some context is necessary to make sense of the -- of what the witness is about to say. But only to make sense of what the witness is about to say. And here the identified adjudicated fact is one where the line of questions, we agree, Mr. Pantelic, is totally unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to turn to events on the 6th of August, 1992. Do you recall where you were being detained at Omarska on the 6th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was detained at different places. For a while I was in the so-called Mujo's Room, that was a room behind the cafeteria. And then for five or six days I was in garage which was next to that room. And on 6 August -- well, actually, I believe the previous night I slept -- or, rather, I didn't really sleep because in that garage the width was about 22, 23, square metres large and there were about 150 and 170 of us, so we were all standing like sardines. Then there was a roll-call. We were among the first, and we boarded the first two or three buses, and we didn't know where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned there was a roll-call. Who gave the roll-call?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The police officers who were taking us away. I'm not sure if it was Meakic or one of the guards. There was one who we called Brki. They made roll-calls the previous days. And on that morning, they called the first group. That's what they called us. I don't know "the first group." The first group of what? And then we boarded the first buses that were lined up in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When they were doing this roll-call, did they have lists with them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They couldn't have called us without them. So they had lists, and they told us that we were the first group. Again, I don't know on which criteria they decided that they were the first group. And there were rumours that we would be exchanged, and all sorts of rumours. But it was clear that we would be taken somewhere but we had no idea where. So we were called as the first group, we boarded the buses. And as far as I could tell, there was a number of buses, ten or 15. The first three or four, maybe five, buses carried the first group. But nobody had told us where we were going nor why. Actually, we were only too glad and could hardly wait to leave that hell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit more about these lists. Were you aware that the police at Omarska were placing people into -- or detainees into categories?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, are we still in the context of Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I really do object to this -- that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We are on the day that they're being taken to Manjaca camp. And the witness has talked about there was a roll-call and there were some lists, and I'm trying to clarify what information those lists contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Olmsted. You're trying to determine circumstances in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, the witness said, himself, he doesn't know about the lists at all. He said I assume they had a list because they wouldn't know on -- by their memory of our names; so therefore I don't see the basis for even asking this question, let alone that it doesn't concern anything about the adjudicated fact this witness is -- has come to give evidence about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I really think it's time for all of us to travel to Manjaca. I mean, let's go to that -- let's go to this particular event. Otherwise, we shall object on numerous bases here because this particular fact you're not allowed. It's 861. And then you're, through the backdoor, trying to get these answers. It's not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'm moving on, Your Honours, any way. But, again, I think it's important to know who was there on the morning of the 6th August, 1992, and what was going on before they entered onto the buses to go to Manjaca. And that's what I -- all I'm trying to do at this stage. But I'll move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were -- you boarded buses. Were you ordered to board those buses, and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. It was the guards who called us, who ordered us to do so. And there were several guards and police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These guards that ordered you to enter the bus, what uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were, I believe -- well, I'll ask you again because I don't see it right here in front of me. How many buses were at Omarska camp that morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: My estimate would be about 15. Or more, maybe. 15-ish. Or, rather, let me say, 15 at least. From 15 to 20. I didn't count them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many detainees do you estimate were on these approximately 15 buses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: When we came to Manjaca, we learned that there were 1300 detainees. That was a known fact, that there were about 1300 of us who were taken to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, either that morning or afterwards, did the police guards from the camp tell you where you were going that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many detainees were on your particular bus that morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on that bus where I was, there were at least 80 or 90 of us. That was a public transportation bus. It wasn't a long-distance bus but one of those commuting buses. And we didn't sit there or stand. We lay on the floor. One on the other, and that is on -- in two layers, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why were you laying on the floor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to. They ordered us to lie down on the floor, one over the others, as -- because we were supposed to pass through the city of Banja Luka, and they wanted the bus to appear empty. We -- we knew the route from Prijedor, and we concluded that we were moving toward Banja Luka. And to anybody who would look -- who would see the buses, the buses would seem empty. Before that, we had all eaten something rotten. It may have been beans or something. So but -- everybody had dysentery and we all stank like animals. And the ones were lying on the others and the police officers would step on our backs to go from -- from the front to the rear, and commenting, Now these Balja guys really stink like hell. And it was very hot. And our filth was usually running down our legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned police officers on the buses. Can you tell us how many police officers were on each bus or if -- to the extent you know, on your bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: On our bus, I think there was only one who was sitting in front. So he was some two metres away from us, and we were all crammed in the rear. And it really stank very badly. I suppose they may not have smelled it. But we were able to make out that there was some sort of escort, but we couldn't see much. Occasionally when one would raise his head to cast a glance outside, then we would see something, but we couldn't determine where we were going. And there was some escort. We saw police vehicles, blue vehicles with police or milicija on them. They seemed like armoured vehicles. But there were also regular cars that escorted us. And it was a rather long drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other than the police escorts that escorted these 15 buses that day, did you see any other organs escorting the buses that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any other escort. I told you that there was a police escort. It seemed like a police armoured vehicle. We saw it when we arrived at Manjaca. There was also some sort of escort, but we couldn't see much of it. There was some regular passenger cars. But I told you, we lay on the floors, underneath the seats, so we were not allowed to raise our heads, and so we didn't really do that. And we were lying on the floor, the ones on the others, like sardines.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned it was hot inside the bus. Can you explain why it was hot inside the bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, 6 August 1992 was a very hot day. And, secondly, all the windows were closed. They didn't allow us to open them even a little. And the heating was also turned on. So there must have been at least 50 degrees inside. It was an inferno. We were all melting away in that heat and in that stench.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, do you personally have any medical conditions that made it particularly bad for you, this bus ride?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Even then, just like today, I'm a diabetic. They didn't give us any water, and I got very thirsty. So it was very hard on me. There wasn't any water. It was unbearably hot. My only desire was to approach the window-panes and lick them because there was condensed water on the window-panes. There was -- the steam condensed upon the window-panes, and it was my wish to get to the window and lick it because there was this small quantity of water there, and that may actually have saved me. Although, then, my sugar level probably dropped considerably, I had lost 30 kilograms, I was starved, and that also may have saved me. And I licked that glass pane on which there was some condensed water, and that's how I was able to ingest some fluid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where did the buses end up that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: During the ride, the buses stopped several times, but we didn't go out. We were lying on the floor. They would open the doors, and they stopped at roadside inns that we noticed as much. We didn't get up. But the locals threw stones at us through the open doors and cursed us. And around 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening it had already -- it was already dark. We arrived at place, we didn't know where we were, but that was in front of the Manjaca camp. And the buses parked there. The drivers had gotten out. And the escort that was on the buses also went out. They again checked whether everything was well closed and the heating was left on, and that's how they left us on those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't think I see this question initially as to when the buses took off, but can you -- from Omarska camp, but perhaps you could tell us, how long did the trip take from Omarska until your arrival at Manjaca? If could you give us an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The trip started at 10.00 a.m. until 8.00 or 9.00 p.m., so it was about 11 hours. We didn't know what time it was though. We didn't know where we were. We were only in that unbearable inferno on those buses. This -- there was immense heat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that they left you on the buses that -- which were sealed and had the heat on. And how long were you made to stay on the buses that night?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: All night. We stayed there all night, until about 6.00 a.m., when it started dawning. Then they opened the doors and ordered us to get out. It was a rather cold at that hour. And from that terrible heat, we suddenly were thrown into this cold morning air.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to talk about events during that night of 6 August to 7 August 1992. During that night, what were the police escorts doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I have to object. The witness just testified that the drivers of the buses -- the drivers of the buses and the escorts left. I don't -- I don't see where does Mr. Olmsted founds the foundation for posing this question. Not to mention that everything we heard so far has nothing do with the adjudicated facts which are about to hear, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is exactly to deal with the denied adjudicated facts. I'll clarify that matter. I appreciate the intervention from my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you clarify for us. You mentioned that the police escorts and drivers left, exited the buses that night. Did they leave the vicinity or did they stay around the buses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed near the buses. We could hear voices, we could hear sounds. Although the engines were running and we were sealed inside those buses, but we could tell that there were others present outside the buses. We didn't know where they were exactly, but we heard that they were around. And they started calling the names of some people on my bus. They started looking for people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you say "they were calling people from your bus," do you know, were those the escorts, or were they someone else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the people who escorted us. From my bus, they took out an elderly man. He was called Dedo Crnalic. And they said, Dedo Crnalic, come out. We heard them opening the door and calling Dedo Crnalic. And they said, We'll make "cevapcici" of him. At that moment he even grabbed my jacket because when we were going to the guards, we were want to put our jackets on because it's less painful when they beat you if you wear a jacket. And then they started beating him immediately. We could hear him groan. And he groaned and whined. And then the sounds died down. And then they threw him back in the bus, and they asked two others to come out. And Dedo Crnalic died there, lying with us in that bus. But we didn't know that until the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When he came back into the bus or he was brought back into the bus, did you have a chance to observe what kind of condition he was in?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: He was -- well, I saw him lying there in the front part of the bus, but I didn't approach him. But I heard him making some sounds, so he must still have been alive. But he -- I didn't pay much attention to him anymore. I was licking the window-panes to -- and I was focussed on my own survival. But he was lying in the front part of the bus. But nobody could leave their place, you know. No one could go to him to see whether he was all right. In the morning, I told some younger guys, Take Dedo out. And they replied, He's dead; he isn't showing any signs of life. And eventually he was taken out, and we saw some other dead bodies lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move on to other victim of this incident, so perhaps this is a good time for us to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, do you recall any other detainees who were taken off of the bus that night?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were many of us, and all of these were people that were familiar. I can't say -- I don't quite understand your question. There were many of us. There were 1.300 detainees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, let me rephrase my question. You already told us about what happened to Mr. Crnalic. And my question to you is: Are you aware of any other detainees who were on the bus that night, the night of 6 August 1992, who were taken off by police guards?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The following morning, we saw some dead bodies, and we got information that Nezir Krak, whom I also knew, and then a neighbour of mine, Sead Babic, called Djuzin, and some other people from other bus were killed. From my bus, Dedo Crnalic was the only one who was killed. But we could see them taking out these other dead bodies from the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned Nezir Krak. During the night, did you hear him being taken out of the buses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was taken out, and then we could see dead bodies there. He never entered Manjaca with us, and we found out that he had been killed. We saw the dead bodies. I didn't get close but there were some seven or eight bodies that were lying there next to the buses, and it was known. We heard when the commander of the camp said, I don't want the dead; I am accepting only the live ones. Because the guards wanted to leave the dead bodies there, and this man Bozidar Popovic said, We are not interested in that. I'm not interested in the dead people; I'm only admitting those who are alive. And so we saw those seven or eight dead bodies. I didn't know all of them. I knew some of them. I knew Nezir Krak well. He was a car mechanic by profession. I would see him often. I would say hello, greet him. We were not friends particularly, but we were not on bad terms either. And I heard and I saw him as being among the dead there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and let me rephrase my question one more time, as I'm trying to get to a particular issue. While you were on the buses on the night of 6/7 August 1992, did you hear the police guards calling out Mr. Krak to come off the bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: We were not able to hear much because the buses were well-closed. They took Dedo Crnalic off our bus. And I must say, truthfully, I didn't hear. I mean, there was some people being called out, some people were looking for some people. We heard that. But it's been 15 years or more since then, so I really cannot say. They were calling out some people. We heard scuffling and sound of voices. But we couldn't hear anything distinctly. But it's a fact that they were taking some people off the buses, looking for some people. The buses were well-closed and we were lying on the floor, so we really couldn't know who was actually being called out. But we heard and then saw the next day some seven or eight dead bodies, and we were told Nezir is there and this Sead Babic and some others that I cannot recall right now were among them. But many of them, seven or eight, were taken off the buses that night and killed, just like Dedo Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that saw the bodies, the corpses, when you got off the bus. Who put the corpses -- who had taken the corpses off the buses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The prisoners, the young men among us. They took the dead bodies from the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know, were they ordered to do that; and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The guards, the policeman, ordered that they be taken out. And that is why Bozidar Popovic reacted, the one who was admitting us to the camp. I said, I don't need dead ones, take that away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That morning, the morning of the 7th of August, when you exited the bus, did you recognise any of the police guards or escorts from the day before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I recognised some policemen. I noticed Bosko Grabez. He was an older reserve policeman, retired. I knew a few others. One of them even spoke to me and he asked me, Mursel is that you? I said, yes, it is, and so on. And then I left quickly. So I don't know if this was wise or not. I didn't really look at the policemen that much. I knew they were policemen. Some of them I [Realtime transcript read in error "you"] knew, some of them I didn't know. The best thing was not to look at them, cross your -- meet their gaze. The biggest problem was that I knew quite a few of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned, I believe, someone by the name of Sead --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just for the accuracy of the transcript, 33:6, I believe the witness said I -- I -- people knew me much -- much more people knew me than I knew them. So ... If can you clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, that's a fairly minor point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But can you confirm that's what you told us just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that these were people, policemen, in police uniforms. I knew some of them. I didn't know all of them. Some were from the surrounding villages. They were not from town itself. Prijedor is a big town, a big municipality, that had 112.407 citizens before the war, so it's logical I didn't know all of them, I didn't all of the policemen. But I knew many of them, and many of them knew me. I was a deputy, I was born in town, I was a well-known caterer, and before that I worked in the school as a teacher, professor. So I assume that many more people knew me. There was some of the pupils there as well. So many more people knew me than I knew them. Some of them you lose sight of. I knew some policemen. I knew that some of them were policemen. I didn't know the names of some of those policemen, but did I know that they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned a police officer by the name Bosko Grabez, G-r-a-b-e-z. Can you tell us, what did you see him doing that morning of the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed about him -- I saw him. I did see him. I knew him well. I knew where he lived. I knew -- he was a policeman, a traffic policeman, even, when he was working as an active policeman. He was older. When I say older, I mean that he was at least ten years older than me. And allegedly he -- this Sead Babic got off the bus, called Djuzin - that was his nickname - with whom this Grabez alledgedly -- well, this Sead would often make jokes at the expense of Bosko. And then that morning there was this incident when this Grabez told some younger policemen, indicating Sead Babic, he pointed him out to these younger policemen, and they took him somewhere, and they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you see Grabez interacting with these two police officers and gesturing towards Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him talking and indicating that they should separate him. There were many of us there. You know, it was difficult to follow. But I noticed that he pointed with his finger at Babic and he asked this younger policeman to take him a little bit further away. And he never entered -- I didn't see Babic dead, even though he was my very close neighbour, close to my house. But he never entered the Manjaca camp with us. He wasn't in the Manjaca camp, which means that he didn't leave this place alive. They took him away. And then there was talk amongst us that Bosko paid him back for some kind of earlier incident, because he would make fun of him. He would joke at his expense when he retired. So this is how this other guy paid him back for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you -- you mentioned that you saw approximately eight corpses near the buses that morning. Can you tell us, did you learn what happened to those corpses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately -- well, the same thing happened to them as with Dedo Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were those corpses taken away that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Bozidar Popovic, the camp commander at Manjaca, to accept the dead bodies. The corpses were later put back on the buses, and according to my information, these bodies were exhumed in 1998, 1999, 2000. And specifically this Dedo Crnalic, whom I knew well, he was an elderly gentleman. Those corpses were not accepted at the Manjaca camp. They were taken back to the buses. This is a fact. And we exhumed Dedo's body in Srbac, which is below Banja Luka. It's about -- it's below Banja Luka, because these bodies were thrown into the Vrbas River. As they were returning from Manjaca, they threw the corpses into the river, and then down river they were buried somewhere, and then we exhumed them. And then after 2000, the family asked for the bodies, and he was exhumed, identified, and buried at the request of the family. I attended the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How long did you remain at Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Manjaca until the 14th or the 15th of November. From the 6th of August, we entered on the 7th, in the morning, and I left Manjaca - I was the oldest in my group, the first group that left - on the 14th. The night between the 14th and the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we had spent some 100 days there, until the 15th of November, when, through the mediation of the Red Cross, we were transferred to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, that was the 14th or 15th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now during your time at the Manjaca camp, did any police officers, civilian police officers, interview you about what had happened to the detainees on the night of the 6th and 7th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity to speak about that. But there was some policemen there, reserve policemen, who were from Sanski Most. I'm not from Sanski Most, but I was with friends from Sanski Most, so one of these policemen that they knew from Sana, we were sitting there in the kitchen talking and he said that those dead bodies were returned also and thrown into the Vrbas River. But I didn't have too many contacts nor did I speak too much about these reserve policemen who were guarding us. Because they were mines around, even one man lost a leg. So it was a problem to stay in one place for too long or to move around, even though I must say that the situation in Manjaca was much better than the situation in Omarska, because the Red Cross came, they gave us blankets, food, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned these police officers from Sanski Most. Do you know, while they were at the camp, were they investigating this particular incident, this crime committed against Mr. Crnalic and the other detainees who were killed outside of Manjaca camp, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It's beyond the issue of the adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody ever took anyone. Oh, sorry, nobody ever investigated the matter, not why we were there, why people were killed, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Murselovic. In view of all the things that you have experienced and all the things that you have gone through, I would like to express Mr. Zupljanin's sympathy. And now I will have to ask you about some details about what you are testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one question: You are still performing a duty in the Prijedor municipality, I assume?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No. In this mandate which is running out, I was a deputy in the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There were recent elections. Were you re-elected?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not run for that level. I was running for the post of president or, rather, vice-president, of the Republika Srpska, and the results have not been published yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, we hope that you will be successful. Mr. Murselovic, when you left Manjaca, you went to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: We were transferred to Karlovac; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's enough you can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At a later period, you came to Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which year was that in?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: This was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You returned to Prijedor after the Dayton Agreement was signed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I came back to Prijedor after the first multi-party elections in 1997. The elections were held in November 1997, and already in October, November, December I had come back to Prijedor in order to set up this new multi-party authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1997, you provided a statement to the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After that, you testified in two cases here, as you said earlier. If you can just say yes or no for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In the Stakic and Brdjanin cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the period from this incident at Manjaca until 1997, did you give a statement to authorised investigative organs of the Federation, or some foreign services, relating to the incidents that you witnessed in Manjaca; did you provide any such statements?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Immediately when we were brought to Karlovac, all of us inmates passed through an interview. We called it an interview. During the first seven or eight days, we had to provide blood and urine samples, go through an examination, and then representatives of international organisations interviewed us. I don't know who those people were, but all of us had to go through this process. And we spoke about all the things that we had experienced. This was in Karlovac, in a barracks somewhere in town. I don't remember exactly where it was. It was somewhere in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And did you sign the statement that provided at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember in 1992 whether I signed it or not. They wanted to have some facts from us, where we were, where did we go, what we experienced, and so on and so forth. All of us who came from the Manjaca camp had to give these statements. Well, we thought this was kind of strange, funny. We were all traumatised, frustrated, so we did give a statement, all of us. This was when we were released. This was sometime in November or December 1992, and it took place in Karlovac. We probably did sign something, but I really cannot remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I know that it's been quite some time ago. At the time, did you refer to the Manjaca incident when you gave this statement, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. I probably did. Because all the things that were important I did mention them. I mean, this interview took a whole day. They asked everybody something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival to Sanski Most in 1995, did you give a statement to the police, the investigators, to the AID, or anybody else about your experience at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you took over your new office in 1995, I think you were also the -- a deputy in the Assembly of RS?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was president of the municipality of Prijedor, or -- and vice-president too. And then I also -- later on I also became a member of parliament, and I was elected three times to the Assembly of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I suppose that as a deputy, as a politician, to this day you haven't officially initiated proceedings or taken part in proceedings against the Serb perpetrators who, according to your knowledge, have committed crimes. You haven't filed criminal complaints or contacted any authority; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't for the simple reason that I had actually faired well as I have survived. So I didn't give it much thought. I thought that -- or, rather, I felt that my -- the mere fact that I was alive was a reward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you certainly don't know, considering what you went through, whether or not the police of the RS initiated criminal proceedings regarding the incidents the Manjaca. You don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. But let me tell you, two or three years ago, I was summoned by the Banja Luka Public Prosecutor's Office to give a statement in my capacity as a member of parliament due to the fact that I was a participant of some events that happened at Manjaca. The prosecutor, whose name I forget, examined me, and I related to him my experiences regarding Dedo Crnalic and some others. So I did make a statement, and I was examined fairly. So whatever I said here today, I also said to that prosecutor. And that may have been two or three years ago, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You and I and everybody from the region know where Banja Luka is, but let's state it for the record any way. You gave a statement to the prosecutor of the RS whose seat is in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us return to some details, Mr. Murselovic. These details are not essential for the Defence of our client because there is no direct relation between him and those individuals down there. But since the Prosecutor asked you, let me ask you the following: You left Banja Luka in that convoy to Manjaca on 6 August 1992, and you testified here today that you stopped several times on the -- on the way there and that you witnessed some hatred and intolerance on the part of some Serb families who had thrown stones at you; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They stopped mostly by roadside inns, I suppose, yes, on our way to Manjaca, and that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But the point is it was war, 1992. The front line is all around. Everybody is dying, Serbs, Croats, Muslims; and there is tension among the Serbs and an unfavorable attitude toward other ethnicities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And there were provocations such as stones being thrown at the convoy by the Serb population; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the logical possibility that the organiser of the convoy and those who provided security to it in order to reduce the risk and possibly avoid provocations ordered you to lie down so that your heads may not be seen. Do you allow for that possibility for -- as being the reason for your position during the transportation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the trip to Manjaca, you said it was stuffy and that everything was closed and that the heating was on and that it was warm outside; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And certainly the driver who was a Serb and the police officers who provided security to you had to bear the same condition as you; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. But the driver could open the window which was next to him, and we were in no position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, my -- I'm asking you logically whether those escorting you would want to make life difficult for themselves by making it unbearable for you. Isn't that illogical? You may have exaggerated some things?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, I most certainly haven't. That was the most difficult day of my life, this trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us return to that convoy. Did they demand any money or some valuables? I mean those who escorted you in -- in that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in the convoy. Because we had been robbed earlier in Omarska, so there was no need to do so because we were left with nothing. But upon arriving at Manjaca we got searched once more. And if anybody had his personal ID on him or anything of the kind, they would take it away at Manjaca, if it was left on somebody at Omarska. Because at Omarska people came in at different hours and under different conditions. But at Manjaca, we were once again searched. They took away all our personal IDs, and that's how it was. And during the ride, there was no need to demand money or valuables from us because at Omarska they had stripped us of everything. At the time, the Seiko 5 watch was very much in vogue, and I found it funny that we were constantly asking whether anybody had a Seiko 5 watch. Obviously to the guards this was something very valuable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience as an eye-witness, you will agree with me when I say that the basic motive of this blackmailing or the extortion of prosperous citizens was robbery, to get something out of the people; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Right. But that possibility was provided them. Nobody prevented them from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you came to Manjaca, you knew some people from your escort, and there's evidence that -- showing that they were also -- they also knew who they wanted from those buses; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So at that moment you were unaware of the motivation of the perpetrator, why they wanted a certain individual from the bus; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You spoke about an episode, but you allow for the possibility that there were some earlier incidents that may have resulted in acts of revenge, as inappropriate as that revenge may be?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At Manjaca, it was a POW camp commanded by the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because that man Bozidar Popovic was a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were at Manjaca earlier, taking part in military exercises; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not at the camp itself. It was a cattle farm. But I was very near that place at Manjaca, as a reserve soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the right of that compound, there's a road and then there's a ditch and so on. But what -- and where were the buses located with regard to the compound?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Now, there are these barns on the right side, and the buses were parked on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was there a -- a large, free space?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, probably. Because there were many buses. But I was so exhausted, and everybody else was, that we didn't have the nerve to look around a lot. And we were eager to get away from those fellow Prijedor people, to call them that, and even if it meant going to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was night, and visibility was poor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the windows were misted up; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it was difficult to see, in such conditions, who did what outside the buses, what kind of incidents went on; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you can assume some details and possibly later under more favourable conditions you may have learned more details. You didn't eye-witness everything; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said as much. But I saw the event with Dedo. I saw him being taken away, and I saw him beaten up when he was brought back, and I saw him dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you cannot be sure about the others; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I did see dead bodies in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the late Mr. Crnalic died on the bus; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your subsequent humanitarian work and social activities or, rather, socio-political activities, at Sanski Most, on several occasions you approached the court, the municipal court at Sanski Most, to make statements about some persons having died, to enable their families to exercise their rights; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it's logical that if you make a statement five years after the incident, that is, in 1997, that such a statement is much more reliable than any statement that you are making now; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, I'm not trying to vivisect you, certainly; I'm merely saying that logically at that time your memory must have been better and that your answers were more detailed. So I'm not trying to trap you in any way, God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document 2D03-1259, please. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Although the letters are very small, I'll take you through some of the details mentioned here. This is a court ruling dated 7 February 1997. We're talking about the Sanski Most Municipal Court. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it's a ruling to declare Dedo Crnalic dead. You can see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
